strengths: Well-motivated and systematic formalization of evaluation protocols (R1, H1, H2, H3, T1, T2) addressing real comparability issues across different ASR systems and model types
Comprehensive experimental design with stratified analysis across multiple dimensions: transcript quality, audio encoders, duration, speaker composition, and detailed hand-crafted feature ablations

Strong empirical insights from research questions, particularly: ASR quality doesn't directly predict segmentation performance, pause duration accounts for ~95% of acoustic feature gains, and clear identification of duration/speaker composition effects on model performance
AudioSeg substantially outperforms text-based approaches on shorter audio (<30 min) by directly leveraging learned audio representations without requiring transcription
High reproducibility with detailed appendices covering hyperparameters, feature extraction methodology, prompts, augmented dataset annotations, and commitment to release code
weaknesses: Single-dataset evaluation (YTSeg, English only, YouTube-specific) severely limits generalizability. Authors acknowledge YTSeg is currently the only large-scale dataset, but this undermines confidence in methodological recommendations and findings applicability

Limited technical novelty: AudioSeg architecture is straightforward (frozen encoder → local transformers → document encoder); performance is heavily encoder-dependent (Whisper Large F1=45.52 vs. Qwen3-AuT F1=24.66), suggesting gains derive primarily from encoder choice rather than architecture

Modest practical improvements without statistical significance testing: AudioSeg shows ~5-8 F1 point gains over text-based models overall, but performance converges for longer content (F1=13.28 vs. 15.17 at ≥60 min); hand-crafted features yield only +3.0 F1 total

AudioSeg performance degradation on longer audio (>20-30 min) is observed but inadequately explained and unresolved. Hypothesis about training data distribution lacks supporting evidence; potential architectural solutions unexplored

MLLM evaluation is limited and underwhelming: restricted to <30 minute videos due to context constraints, weak baseline performance (Qwen2.5-Omni: F1=3.43), and LoRA fine-tuning produces severe hallucinations (1032.6% transcript length). Claims about MLLM promise are overstated

Proposed time-based evaluation protocols (T1, T2) lack complete empirical validation: Table A6 shows T1 maintains ranking consistency with existing text-space protocols (somewhat undermining necessity argument); T2 (continuous-time) is never experimentally evaluated despite being the most novel contribution
No cross-validation, multiple runs with different seeds, or statistical significance tests despite some improvements being modest, limiting confidence in reported gains

Non-speech audio cues (music, sound effects) validated only through single ablation (Table A1: -2.21 F1 with DeepFilterNet). Insufficient analysis of when and how much this contributes to AudioSeg's advantage

strengths: Well-motivated problem addressing genuine limitations of transcript-centric chaptering approaches, with clear articulation of challenges (ASR errors, discretization loss, sentence boundary snapping)
Comprehensive systematic evaluation framework formalizing multiple evaluation protocols (R1, H1, H2, H3, T1, T2) that enable transcript-invariant comparison—a useful methodological contribution

Extensive empirical evaluation across multiple dimensions: transcript quality effects, acoustic features, duration/speaker composition, 5+ audio encoders, multiple model architectures, with good stratified analysis
Dataset augmentation contribution adding duration regimes, speaker regimes, and ASR variants to YTSeg for future research
Strong reproducibility: detailed hyperparameters, feature extraction procedures, model prompts, and promised code release
Honest reporting of limitations and negative results (MLLM weaknesses, AudioSeg degradation on long audio)
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: AudioSeg is straightforward hierarchical transformer applied to audio chunks with no novel architectural contributions; hand-crafted features are standard prosodic features; evaluation protocols are incremental refinements of existing work (T1 applies existing metrics to time discretization; T2 uses collar-based F1 from sound event detection)

Critical single-dataset limitation: all experiments on YTSeg only (English-only, 19k videos), with no cross-dataset validation or generalizability testing—severely problematic for ACL where broader applicability is expected

AudioSeg's core result is methodologically questionable: best performance (F1=45.52) uses Whisper Large, an ASR encoder that encodes linguistic information from audio; this undermines the 'audio-only' framing since models access linguistic structure via the encoder rather than truly avoiding transcripts; non-ASR encoders (HuBERT: F1=35.58) perform substantially worse, approaching text-based performance

MLLM evaluation severely limited and underwhelming: results restricted to <30min audio due to context length; Qwen3-Omni ICL achieves only F1=41.30 (lower than AudioSeg); self-cascaded experiments confirm obvious findings without novel insights

Insufficient analysis of core findings: (1) Q1's 'weak WER-performance correspondence' is noted but not explained; (2) non-speech cues finding is anecdotal with modest DeepFilterNet ablation (-2.21 F1); (3) why Whisper vastly outperforms other encoders is speculated but not systematically investigated; (4) AudioSeg's sharp degradation beyond 20-30 minutes lacks thorough explanation

Evaluation protocol implementation inconsistency: despite proposing T1/T2 as superior, results primarily reported in T1 (still discretized time); if time-space protocols are better, why not commit to them fully? Oracle experiment shows 73-81% ceiling motivating time-based evaluation but this isn't fully leveraged

No statistical significance testing: no error bars, confidence intervals, or significance tests; claimed improvements (45.52 vs 40.01) might not be statistically significant given potential dataset variance
Limited ablations: no systematic investigation of AudioSeg architectural choices (why 30s chunks, 6s windows, 1-layer local transformer?); these appear somewhat arbitrary
Unclear practical impact: ~5 F1 improvement on short audio; performance degrades or reverses on longer audio (>30min); MLLMs underperform; actionable takeaway unclear
Missing comparisons with acoustic feature-based topic segmentation from prior work (Lai et al. 2016, 2020); limited engagement with broader segmentation literature

strengths: Well-motivated problem with clear identification of limitations in existing transcript-centric approaches; strong articulation of domain mismatch between continuous-time boundaries and discrete units

Novel evaluation protocol formalization (R1, H1, H2, H3, T1, T2) that enables fair, transcript-invariant comparison across heterogeneous modeling paradigms; this methodological contribution is valuable beyond model development

Comprehensive and systematic experimental design with structured research questions (Q1-Q4), rich dataset augmentation (duration/speaker/ASR variants), extensive ablations and stratified analyses validating findings robustly

Strong empirical finding that learned audio representations (AudioSeg with Whisper Large: F1=45.52) substantially outperform text-based approaches (MiniSeg+Features: F1=40.30), challenging transcript-centric paradigm
Excellent reproducibility: comprehensive hyperparameters, feature extraction methodology, all prompts, and promised code/dataset release establishing high standards for transparency
Honest and detailed limitations discussion acknowledging single-dataset scope, English-only evaluation, and computational constraints; transparent about MLLM computational barriers
weaknesses: Severe generalizability limitations: all claims rest on single dataset (YTSeg); acknowledged as only available large-scale chaptering dataset; no cross-dataset validation or investigation of domain-specific factors; Whisper Large's strong performance likely benefited by YouTube training data similarity, not fully explored

AudioSeg's reliance on proprietary Whisper Large encoder with dramatic performance variance across encoders (HuBERT Large F1: 35.58 vs Whisper F1: 45.52) raises questions about whether finding reflects architectural novelty vs. pre-training quality; architecture itself (chunk→encode→aggregate→segment) is relatively straightforward with limited ablations

Concerning performance degradation contradicts core claims: AudioSeg F1 drops from 50.01 (<10min) to 13.28 (≥60min); text-based models become competitive at ≥60min; severely limits practical applicability for long-form content despite being key motivation

MLLM evaluation underdeveloped and weak: restricted to <30min videos; only two models tested; LoRA fine-tuning causes severe hallucinations (1032% transcript length); Qwen3-Omni only marginally outperforms AudioSeg (F1: 41.30); instruction-following issues identified but not deeply investigated; claims of MLLMs being 'promising' lack support

Shallow acoustic feature analysis: pause duration dominates (+2.87 F1); other features contribute minimally with no feature importance ranking or statistical significance testing; pitch/speaking rate show zero improvement without investigation; modest overall acoustic gains (+3.0 F1) suggest hand-crafted features are not primary drivers

Evaluation protocol validation incomplete: T2 (continuous-time) proposed as 'most direct' but never experimentally evaluated; no ranking consistency comparison between T1 and T2; divergence in Table A6 (MiniSeg Ref R1: 43.37 vs T1: 39.54) raises questions about protocol equivalence; oracle ceiling (73-81%) indicates substantial task difficulty but no inter-annotator agreement provided

Limited error analysis and investigation: only footnote reference to non-speech cues where AudioSeg excels; comprehensive error categorization absent; multi-speaker challenges shown in Figure 3 but not deeply analyzed; no baseline comparisons (e.g., pause-only segmentation despite identifying pauses as key feature)

Design choices insufficiently justified: 6-second windows justified only by 'average sentence length' without sensitivity analysis; 30-second chunk sizes for frame encoding not ablated; no statistical significance testing, confidence intervals, or stratified cross-validation despite large performance variance

Unexplained methodological anomalies: MiniSeg trained on lower-WER ASRL performs worse than ASRT across most conditions, contradicting WER-performance relationship; explanation offered but not rigorously investigated; suggests ASR errors affect segmentation in non-obvious ways requiring deeper analysis

Long-content failure represents fundamental limitation for stated use cases (podcasts, lectures, videos); short-duration dominance (Figure 2) undermines practical applicability; training data underrepresentation of long content acknowledged but not resolved

strengths: Clear problem motivation addressing real gaps in existing transcript-centric audio chaptering research
Formalized evaluation protocols (T1, T2) that enable fair transcript-invariant comparison across modeling paradigms—a solid methodological contribution
Comprehensive experimental design systematically addressing five clear research questions with stratified analysis by duration, speaker regime, and domain
Significant reproducibility contribution: large-scale dataset (19.3K videos) with duration/speaker annotations, detailed hyperparameters, feature extraction methodology, and promised toolkit release

Actionable empirical findings: pause duration dominates acoustic gains (+2.87 F1); speaker features provide targeted improvements (+2.95 F1 in multi-speaker); joint training on reference+ASR improves robustness
Well-organized writing with clear motivation, methods, and presentation of results
weaknesses: Severe dataset limitation: primary reliance on YTSeg (YouTube, English-only); AMI validation uses only 25 evaluation videos; poor cross-domain transfer (Qwen3 F1: 41.30→9.16) suggests findings are YouTube-specific and lack generalizability

AudioSeg's source of improvement unclear: performance varies dramatically by encoder (Whisper Large 45.52 vs HuBERT 35.58 vs PEA-Frame 31.36), suggesting encoder choice (with domain match to YouTube) drives results, not architectural novelty; architecture itself is standard

Evaluation protocol may favor AudioSeg: T1 uses 6-second chunks matching AudioSeg's native resolution while text models are mapped to this grid; Table A8 shows non-monotonic behavior at non-aligned chunk sizes; oracle analysis (Table A7) shows 20% F1 discretization loss yet is treated as technical detail

MLLM evaluation incomplete: limited to <30 min videos, only Qwen models, task conflates transcription+segmentation+titling, unable to fine-tune Qwen3-Omni due to computational constraints, temporal grounding bottleneck (11.8s median error) unclear whether fundamental or temporary

Acoustic feature analysis underdeveloped: pauses dominate (+2.87 F1) but other features contribute minimally; no statistical significance testing or investigation of why pitch/speaking rate/loudness fail; suggests hand-crafted feature approach may be wrong direction

ASR quality analysis incomplete: weak WER-segmentation correspondence unexplained; counterintuitive finding (ASRL-trained model underperforms ASRT) without investigation; missing analysis of which ASR error types matter for chaptering
Limited technical novelty: text-based contribution is simple concatenation+linear projection of features; AudioSeg architecture is standard; no architectural ablations isolating design choices
No statistical rigor: no confidence intervals, p-values, or multi-run variance analysis despite large dataset; single train/val/test split reported
Title generation under-evaluated: metrics relegated to appendix, two proposed evaluation protocols (TM, GC) lack strong justification, limited discussion of quality-importance tradeoff

Missing ablations and comparisons: no isolation of chunk-size effects on AudioSeg vs text models, limited breadth of text baselines beyond MiniSeg, no comparison with recent audio-based segmentation methods

strengths: Well-formalized evaluation protocols (R1-R3, H1-H3, T1-T2) that address genuine limitations in existing transcript-based evaluation approaches
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple modeling paradigms (text-based, audio-only, MLLMs) with careful dataset augmentation (duration, speaker regimes, multiple ASR transcripts)
Useful practical insights including pause features as dominant acoustic contributor, performance degradation on long-form content, and speaker regime effects on model robustness
Responsible resource release (evaluation toolkit, AudioSeg) and cross-domain validation attempt (though limited) on AMI corpus
Clear presentation with effective visualizations and well-organized experimental design
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty in proposed models: AudioSeg is a straightforward hierarchical application of standard components (frame encoding → segment encoding → document encoding) without architectural innovation

Misleading core claims about AudioSeg: AudioSeg's superior performance (F1: 45.52) critically depends on Whisper Large encoder, which encodes linguistic information. Performance drops to 24-35 F1 with other encoders. This undermines the 'audio-only' framing and suggests encoder choice, not architecture, drives performance.

Weak hand-crafted audio features contribution: Only +0.99 F1 improvement overall, with pause duration driving nearly all gains (+2.87 F1). Claims about non-speech audio cues supported by only 3 cherry-picked examples without systematic validation.

Oversized and underdeveloped MLLM section: Dedicates substantial space (Section 5.3, Table 7, Appendix C) to showing MLLMs perform poorly (F1: 3.43-41.30), yielding limited actionable insights. Temporal grounding failures (11.8s median deviation) suggest fundamentally negative results.

Superficial analysis of key findings: (1) Duration degradation explained only as 'data distribution'—no deeper investigation of root causes or solutions; (2) Counterintuitive ASR quality paradox (better ASR sometimes yields worse segmentation) mentioned but not investigated; (3) Non-speech cues claim based on 3 anecdotal examples, not systematic analysis.

Severe dataset limitations inadequately addressed: Primary reliance on single YTSeg dataset, AMI validation is tiny (9-16 test samples), English-only, and cross-domain generalization is poor (Qwen3 competitive on YTSeg but fails on AMI). Acknowledged limitations not resolved.

Missing critical experimental analysis: No computational cost comparison, no streaming scenario discussion, MLLM experiments artificially capped at <30 min, absent error analysis, no investigation of how chapter density affects performance, no comparison to audio event detection baselines

Incomplete evaluation protocol justification: 6-second chunks chosen only by matching average sentence length without principled criteria; T2 tolerances (±3s, ±6s) selected without justification; T1 ranking consistency with text protocols doesn't validate appropriateness

Reproducibility concerns: Promised code/toolkit unavailable at review time; extensive hyperparameter variations across models (Tables A12-A14); multi-modal preprocessing differences complicate comparisons
Missing ablations: No isolation of Whisper pre-training contribution vs. architecture; no comparison of text-based models using Whisper embeddings; no systematic AudioSeg component ablation

strengths: Well-motivated problem identification: Clearly articulates limitations in prior work regarding evaluation of transcript-dependent vs. transcript-invariant metrics, and temporal vs. text-space boundary alignment.

Significant methodological contribution: Systematization of evaluation protocols (R1, H1, H2, H3, T1, T2) with particular value in formalizing transcript-invariant time-based evaluation for fair cross-model comparison.

Comprehensive experimental design: Multiple modeling paradigms, multiple audio encoders, thorough ablations on acoustic features, stratified analysis by duration/speaker composition, and cross-domain validation.

Strong empirical results: AudioSeg substantially outperforms text-based approaches on typical-length content (F1=51.40 vs. 44.40 for 10-30 min videos), demonstrating complementary value of audio information.

Valuable dataset annotations and resources: Public release of duration regimes, speaker annotations, multiple ASR variants on YTSeg, plus evaluation toolkit and AudioSeg code; clear reproducibility with detailed hyperparameters.

Thorough analysis of acoustic factors: Clear insights on pause duration being the primary driver (+2.87 F1), speaker features helping in multi-speaker contexts, and discovery of non-speech audio importance.
Clear presentation: Well-organized paper with informative figures/tables, comprehensive appendices covering hyperparameters, feature extraction, prompts, and implementation details.
weaknesses: Limited generalizability: Heavy reliance on single dataset (YTSeg, YouTube-only) with cross-domain validation only on small-scale AMI corpus (4-9 test videos); English-only data limits multilingual applicability. This undermines generalizability claims.

Misleading framing of AudioSeg as 'audio-only': Best results (F1=45.52) use Whisper Large, an ASR encoder that captures linguistic structure alongside acoustic patterns. Performance drops substantially with pure acoustic encoders (HuBERT Large F1=35.58, PEA-Frame F1=31.36). The implicit linguistic information from pre-training confounds comparison with text-based approaches.

Significant performance degradation on longer content: AudioSeg drops from F1=51.40 (10-30 min) to F1=13.28 (≥60 min); text-based methods become competitive at longer durations. Attributed to training imbalance and sparse boundaries, but this fundamental task difficulty limits practical applicability.

Limited MLLM evaluation and conclusions: Restricted to <30 min videos due to context constraints; Qwen3-Omni underperforms AudioSeg (F1=41.30); temporal grounding fails catastrophically (median 11.8s deviation); primarily demonstrates MLLMs are not yet competitive without providing solutions.

Statistical rigor lacking: No confidence intervals, significance tests, or discussion of variance across multiple runs. Single train/test split implied. Makes it difficult to assess significance of reported improvements.

Hand-crafted feature fusion is simplistic: Only concatenation + linear projection explored; most gains driven by pause duration alone; modest overall improvements limit the finding about acoustic feature utility.
Limited architectural novelty: AudioSeg uses standard 3-stage pipeline with conventional components (Transformers, RoFormer). While effective, not architecturally innovative.

Evaluation protocol validation incomplete: Primarily uses T1 (discrete time); T2 results in appendix. Oracle segmentation achieves only 73-81% F1 even with perfect boundaries—inherent task ceiling not discussed. Non-monotonic variations in Table A8 attributed to 're-discretization artifacts' deserve deeper investigation.

Fairness of encoder comparisons: AudioSeg benefits from Whisper pre-trained on 680K hours of speech data, while text-based models trained from-scratch on YTSeg. Comparison not entirely fair in terms of total supervision and pre-training data scale.

Limited error analysis: Analysis stratified only by duration/speaker; no qualitative analysis of failure modes; no computational efficiency comparisons; missing simple baselines (e.g., silence-based segmentation).
